source: Northern Territory Government, Department of Resources — Field Guide to Pests, Beneficials, Diseases and Disorders of Mangoes (2nd edition), December 2010, ISBN 978-0-7245-7200-7
text:
Spiders
(Family Salticidae, Thomisidae, Oxyopidae,
Araneidae and many others)
Targeted prey: A large range of flying and crawling insects such as
redbanded thrips, planthoppers, caterpillars and moths.
Description:
Eggs: Eggs are produced in strong silken sacs, or in a silken mass
curled in leaves or on the bark. The eggs are often protected by the
female.
Immatures: Spiderlings are similar to adults but are usually smaller
with variations in colour and markings.
Adults: Spiders have eight legs and two distinct body parts
(cephalothorax and abdomen). They also have simple eyes (usually
8), silk producing organs and no antennae or wings. Spiders are of
various sizes and colour, depending on the species.
Biology and predatory activity: The life cycle is variable according
to the species. Spider webbing can be mistaken for flower caterpillar
webbing. It is believed that spiders are less affected by orchard
spraying than other beneficials. Spiders can be seen on most parts
of the tree such as in flower panicles, on leaves or on the bark. They
are often found in silken webs in curled leaves or in webs between
shoots.
caveat: This source is an Australian (Northern Territory) government field guide, not a Cambodia-specific MAFF publication. It is included as a supplementary international reference for visual identification and general pest/disease biology only. Species presence, seasonal timing (the guide's monthly monitoring calendars reflect the NT dry/wet season cycle), and any pesticide or chemical guidance are specific to northern Australia and may not apply directly to Cambodian conditions, seasons, or registered products. This edition of the source itself does not list specific pesticide products or rates (noted as intentionally omitted pending updated registrations), so none are reported here either.
